subject: Civil Engineering
title: The Quebec Bridge Disasters
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Quebec Bridge Disasters.

hook.text: The Quebec Bridge collapsed twice — in 1907 and again in 1916. 88 workers died total.

buildup.text: In 1907, the chief engineer noticed the steel was bending but didn't stop work.

discovery.text: The south cantilever arm buckled under its own weight — a compression member failed.

twist.text: They rebuilt it with a different design. The center span fell into the river during lifting.

climax.text: The third attempt succeeded in 1919 — the world's longest cantilever bridge.

punchline.text: Two collapses and 88 deaths before they got it right.

quiz.question: How many times did the Quebec Bridge collapse during construction?

details.summary: The Quebec Bridge over the St. Lawrence River collapsed twice during construction, in 1907 killing 75 workers and in 1916 killing 13 more. The first collapse was caused by inadequate design calculations and ignored warning signs of buckling.
details.whyItMatters: The Quebec Bridge disasters led to fundamental reforms in engineering ethics, peer review, and professional accountability. Many engineering schools reference it as a cautionary tale about overconfidence.
takeaways: The 1907 collapse killed 75 workers when compression members buckled
Design errors were compounded by ignored warnings from site engineers
The disasters prompted creation of engineering licensing and ethics codes

faq.question: What specific design error caused the 1907 Quebec Bridge collapse?
faq.answer: Chief engineer Theodore Cooper underestimated the dead load by 18% and did not recalculate stresses when the span was increased from 488 to 549 meters. Critical compression members were overstressed beyond their buckling capacity.

faq.question: How did the Quebec Bridge collapse influence engineering ethics?
faq.answer: Canadian engineers began wearing iron rings forged from Quebec Bridge wreckage steel as reminders of ethical responsibility. Several Canadian provinces established professional engineering licensing requirements as a direct result. The emphasis on independent design review became standard practice.
